summary.description: One or two sentences describing what the diff does and the overall security posture of the change.

findings.description: Security findings introduced or left exploitable by this diff. Empty array when the diff is clean.

severity.description: Your own overall judgement of how bad this is. Recorded for comparison, but the severity the gate acts on is derived from the three factual fields below, not from this one — they are answerable from the code, and this is not.

confidence.description: How certain you are that this is a real, reachable vulnerability rather than a theoretical one.

line.description: Line number in the new version of the file. Use 0 if not attributable to a single line.

evidence.description: The vulnerable code copied verbatim from the file at the cited line — one to five lines. No diff markers, no ellipses, no paraphrasing, no reconstruction from memory. This string is matched against the real file before the finding is accepted, and must identify ONE place in it: a quote that matches several lines is rejected rather than attached to the first one. Quote the whole statement, and surrounding lines when the statement alone is not distinctive.

description.description: What is wrong, referencing the specific added code.

exploit_scenario.description: Concrete attacker path: who sends what input, through which entry point, to what effect. Must be specific, not generic.

recommendation.description: The concrete fix, ideally with the corrected code shape.

impact.description: What the attacker actually achieves. `code_execution`: runs code or commands. `broad_data_access`: reads whole tables, arbitrary files, or other users' records. `narrow_data_access`: reads one specific record or file they were not meant to see. `state_change`: writes, deletes, or performs an action as someone else. `metadata_disclosure`: learns something that only helps a further attack — a path, a version, whether a file exists. `denial_of_service`: makes the service unavailable.

reachable_without_authentication.description: Can an unauthenticated caller reach the vulnerable code? Answer from what you can see: an unauthenticated route, a missing decorator, a public webhook is `yes`; a handler behind a login check is `no`. Use `unclear` when routing or middleware lives outside this repository. `unclear` is a real answer and is treated consistently — guessing is what makes the same finding come out differently on different runs.

requires_user_interaction.description: Must a victim do something for the attack to work — click a link, open a page, upload a file the attacker chose? Reflected XSS and CSRF are `yes`; a direct request to an endpoint is `no`.
